Passwords Using a password manager is advised. A good one should not store the master key on their side — I suggest Bitwarden as it's free, open source, supports 2FA, has clients for all OSes, and extensions for all browsers, and has a self hosted option if you would prefer to not use their server. It can also auto-generate passwords for you per site. 10/10

Encryption On Linux use LUKS or just plain dm-crypt. LUKS uses a header on the disk so it breaks plausible deniability, but if you're an advanced user you can put the header on a USB stick. You can also use dm-crypt which does not install a header (and thus the whole disk looks like random data), but you'll need to remember the encryption parameters (again only for advanced users). It's also possible to setup kill-switches (for example tied to a bluetooth connection) such that the plain text key in memory is wiped if the computer is locked, or you move to far away from the computer (protects against cold boot attacks).

Use UEFI. UEFI is a pain in the ass, but you can create and install your own keys so that your computer will only boot if the bootloader is signed by your private key. Even with compromised hardware, this should prevent "evil maid" attacks.

Use TOR and a VPN... but only all the time, or none of time. Despite the FUD around TOR, it is in fact secure and has not been cracked (even by the NSA), However, it is susceptible to certain out of band attacks, such as timing attacks, and correlation attacks. In addition, connecting to a TOR/VPN IP once in a while is huge flag that says "I'm doing something I want to hide". As such, you should always be connected to prevent timing attacks (and to reduce suspicion).
